lead: The collision regulations settle who keeps clear and how. Ask in order: is there risk of collision, what is she, which rule fits?

sections.title: A steady bearing means risk of collision

qa.q: How can I tell if another boat is on a collision course with me?
qa.a: Take compass bearings of her: a steady bearing with the range closing means **risk of collision**, and in doubt, assume it. Near a big ship the risk can exist even while the bearing changes.

blocks.p: Keep a **lookout** by sight and hearing at all times, under the genoa too. AIS and radar help, but many small boats show on neither. Keep a **safe speed**: able to stop in the distance you can see, slower in traffic, near swimmers or against shore lights.

Take compass bearings of an approaching vessel. A steady bearing with the range closing is **risk of collision**; in doubt, assume it. Near a big ship it can exist even while the bearing changes. Act early: one bold alteration she can see at once, not several small ones. If you cannot turn, slow down or stop, and keep checking until she is past and clear.

qa.q: When two sailing boats meet, which one has to give way?
qa.a: The boat on **port tack**, with the wind on her port side, keeps clear of the one on starboard tack. On the same tack, the windward boat keeps clear.

blocks.p: Of two sailing vessels, the one on **port tack**, with the wind on her port side, keeps clear of the one on starboard tack. On the same tack the **windward** boat keeps clear. On a run, your tack is the side opposite your mainsail.

tiles.name: Opposite tacks

tiles.name: Same tack

blocks.p: On port tack, if you cannot tell the tack of a boat to windward, keep clear. When you stand on, hold your course and speed.

sections.title: Three meetings and the stand-on vessel

qa.q: Who gives way when two motorboats are crossing or meet head-on?
qa.a: Crossing, the vessel with the other on her starboard side gives way and avoids passing ahead; **head-on**, both turn to starboard. An overtaking vessel, sail included, keeps clear until past.

blocks.p: **Overtaking** binds every vessel, sail included: coming up from more than 22.5° abaft her beam, where at night you would see only her sternlight, you keep clear until past. Two power-driven vessels **head-on** both turn to starboard. **Crossing**, the one with the other on her starboard side gives way and avoids passing ahead.

The **stand-on vessel** holds her course and speed. If the other does not act, sound five short blasts; you may then manoeuvre, but under power do not turn to port for a vessel on your port side. Once her action alone cannot prevent a collision, you must act. A big ship may not have seen you and cannot stop quickly.

blocks.rule: In doubt whether you are overtaking or head-on? Assume you are.

qa.q: Does a sailing yacht have right of way over a fishing boat?
qa.a: No: sail and power both keep clear of a vessel **engaged in fishing**, restricted in her ability to manoeuvre or not under command. Otherwise, overtaking apart, a power-driven vessel keeps clear of a sailing vessel.

blocks.p: Overtaking apart, a power-driven vessel keeps clear of a sailing vessel. Both keep clear of a vessel **engaged in fishing**, **restricted in her ability to manoeuvre** or **not under command**, and avoid impeding one constrained by her draught.

With the engine in gear your yacht is **power-driven**, whatever sails are set. Trolling lines is not fishing. An extra white light on a fishing vessel points to her gear: pass the other side. Never pass between a tug and her tow. A vessel aground marks the shoal: stay away.

sections.title: Never impede a ship in her channel

qa.q: How should a yacht cross the shipping lanes of a traffic separation scheme?
qa.a: In a **traffic separation scheme**, cross on a heading at right angles to the lanes, under engine if need be, and keep out of the separation zone.

blocks.p: In a **narrow channel** keep as near its starboard edge as is safe. A sailing vessel or a vessel under 20 m must not impede a ship that can only navigate inside the channel, nor cross ahead of her. That duty remains when risk of collision develops.

In a **traffic separation scheme** follow your lane with the traffic. Join or leave at its ends, or from the side at a small angle. Cross on a heading at right angles to the lanes, under engine if need be, and keep out of the separation zone. A yacht under 20 m may use the inshore zone, but must not impede a power-driven vessel in a lane. Expect converging ships where a scheme ends.

qa.q: What do one, two or three short blasts from a ship's horn mean?
qa.a: From a power-driven vessel in sight, one short blast means she is altering course to starboard, two short to port, three short that her engines are going astern. Five or more short mean she doubts you are keeping clear.

blocks.p: A short blast lasts about a second, a prolonged one four to six. A power-driven vessel in sight of another signals each manoeuvre.

qa.q: Who has right of way in fog when I can only see the other boat on radar?
qa.a: Nobody stands on in **restricted visibility**: each vessel avoids a close-quarters situation. For a vessel seen on radar alone, do not turn to port if she is forward of your beam, nor towards her if she is abeam or abaft it.

blocks.p: Out of sight of each other nobody stands on: each vessel avoids a close-quarters situation. Slow down until you can stop within the visibility. For a vessel seen on radar alone, do not turn to port if she is forward of your beam, nor towards her if she is abeam or abaft it. A fog signal heard forward of the beam means bare steerage way, or stopping. Once she is in sight, the ordinary rules apply.
